initial_observation.demographics: A 78-year-old woman with a known history of hypertensive cardiomyopathy and paroxysmal benign positional vertigo
initial_observation.chief_complaint: 5-day history of throat pain and hoarseness, as well as progressive and dolorous swelling in the submandibular area, progressive coughing, dysphagia for 2 days, and ultimately breathing difficulties
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Body temperature 37.7 °C, haemodynamically stable with slightly hypertensive blood pressure (150/80 mm Hg) and tachycardia (118/min), room-air oxygen saturation above 90%. Blood analysis showed leucocytosis 17.2 g/L and elevated C-reactive Protein (CRP) 125 mg/L.

evidence_items.source_text: The initial clinical examination confirmed the submandibular swelling; the enoral examination was severely limited by a restricted mouth opening. Otoscopic examination was impossible due to ceruminal occlusion. Meningism was ruled out.

Due to a non-conclusive clinical examination and the, although stable, visibly affected patient, a neck CT scan performed with intravenous contrast, which showed the thumbprint sign typical for acute epiglottitis as well as extensive supraglottic and subglottic swelling resulting in stenosis (figure 1).

After returning from the CT scan, the patient’s condition deteriorated within minutes. The oxygen saturation dropped to about 70% and did not recover even with 10 L of O2 administered via reservoir mask. Respiratory exhaustion was imminent. While intravenous Solu-Medrol and Co-Amoxicillin were administered, intubation was initiated, which proved to be extremely difficult due to swelling of the supraglottic soft tissue, although video-guided GlideScope was used. Consequently, the patient went into hypoxaemia and eventually into cardiac arrest. Reanimation protocol was immediately initiated. After even direct tracheal airway access failed, another attempt was made to orally intubate the patient, this time with success. After around 5 min of mechanical reanimation and a total of 2 mg intravenous adrenalin, ROSC was achieved.

During the course of hospitalisation, the initially sampled blood cultures revealed N. meningitidis bacteraemia. The antibiotic regimen was changed from Co-Amoxicillin 2.2 g every 8 hours to ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours. Intravenous steroid application was continued.
The patient remained intubated for a week when a follow-up CT scan showed decreased swelling of the epiglottis while swelling of the larynx and subglottic area remained grossly unchanged.

After 11 days, the respiratory situation had improved enough to cease mechanical ventilation and eventually tracheostomy was reversed. The patient was discharged into a neurorehabilitation facility to properly treat the remaining neurological impairments caused by the initial hypoxic event.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: the cause of the airway obstruction was caused by epiglottitis/supraglottitis due to infection with N. meningitidis
